````math
## Appendix C Omitted Proofs

###### Proposition C.1 ([Cai et al. (2016)](#bib.bib10)).

In CSP games, for any CCE $`\mu`$, if $`i`$ deviates to $`s_{i}`$, then
their expected utility if other players continue to play $`\mu`$ is
equal to their utility if other player where to play the marginal
strategy profile $`s^{\mu}_{-i}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}[u_{i}(s_{i},\rho_{-i})]=u_{i}(s_{i},s^{\mu}_{-i})\ \forall s_{i}\in S_{i}`$ |  |

### C.1 Proof of Proposition [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 4.3. ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")

###### Proposition [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 4.3. ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").

If $`\mu`$ is an $`\epsilon`$-CCE of a CSP game $`G`$, $`s^{\mu}`$ is an
$`n\epsilon`$-Nash of $`G`$.

###### Proof.

Since $`\mu`$ is an $`\epsilon`$-CCE, $`\forall i\in N`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho)\right]\leq\epsilon`$ |  |

which implies (by
Proposition [C.1](#A3.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition C.1 ( ( ) ). ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"))
that $`\forall i\in N`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})-\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho)\right]\leq\epsilon`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\implies`$ | $`\displaystyle\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})\leq\epsilon+\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho)\right].`$ |  |

Summing over $`N`$, we get

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{i\in N}\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i\in N}\left(\epsilon+\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho)\right]\right)`$ |  | (1) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in N}\epsilon+\sum_{i\in N}\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho)\right]`$ |  | (2) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in N}\epsilon+\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}(\rho)\right]`$ |  | (3) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=n\epsilon+c`$ |  | (4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=n\epsilon+\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}(s^{\mu}).`$ |  | (5) |

Where
([4](#A3.E4 "In Proof. ‣ C.1 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"))
and
([5](#A3.E5 "In Proof. ‣ C.1 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"))
use the fact that
$`\forall\rho\in\mathrm{P},\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}(\rho)=c`$ for some
constant. The above inequalities give us

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{i\in N}\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})\leq n\epsilon+\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}(s^{\mu}).`$ |  |

Rearranging, we get

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{i\in N}\underbrace{\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})-u_{i}(s^{\mu})}_{\geq 0}\leq n\epsilon.`$ |  |

All terms in the sum are are non-negative because $`\rho_{i}^{\prime}`$
is a best-response to $`s^{\mu}_{-i}`$. Then any particular term in the
summation is upper bounded by $`n\epsilon`$. ∎

### C.2 Proof of Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Theorem 4.6. ‣ 4.2 Subgame Stability ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")

###### Proposition C.3.

In two-player constant-sum games, for any $`\epsilon`$-Nash equilibrium
$`s`$ and player $`i`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(s)-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}}u_{i}(s_{i},s^{\prime}_{-i})\leq\epsilon.`$ |  |

The proof of
Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3. ‣ C.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
is immediate from the fact that no player can gain more than
$`\epsilon`$ utility by deviating and the game is constant-sum.

###### Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Theorem 4.6. ‣ 4.2 Subgame Stability ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").

Let $`G`$ be a CSP game. If $`G`$ is $`(0,\gamma)`$-subgame stable, then
for any player $`i\in N`$ and CCE $`\mu`$ of $`G`$, we have
$`\textup{Vul}_{i}\left(s^{\mu},S_{-i}\right)\leq|E_{i}|\gamma`$.

###### Proof.

First we show 1. Any marginal strategy $`s^{\mu}`$ of a CCE $`\mu`$ is a
Nash equilibrium of $`G`$ [Cai et al. (2016)](#bib.bib10). Then,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textup{Vul}_{i}\left(s^{\mu},S_{-i}\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq u_{i}(s^{\mu})-\min_{s_{-i}\in S_{-i}}u_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{-i})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}u_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\min_{s_{-i}\in S_{-i}}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}u_{ij}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j})\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}u_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\min_{s_{j}\in S_{j}}u_{ij}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j}).`$ |  |

Where the last line uses the fact that $`-i`$ minimize $`i^{\prime}s`$
utility, so can do so without coordinating since $`G`$ is polymatrix.
Continuing,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\left(u_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\min_{s_{j}\in S_{j}}u_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j})\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\gamma`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq|E_{i}|\gamma,`$ |  |

where by $`(0,\gamma)`$-subgame stability of each $`G_{ij}`$,
$`(s^{\mu}_{i},s^{\mu}_{i})`$ is a $`\gamma`$-Nash of $`G_{ij}`$. By
Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3. ‣ C.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
we have
$`u_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\min_{s_{j}\in S_{j}}u_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j})\leq\gamma`$.
∎

### C.3 Proof of Proposition [4.8](#S4.Thmtheorem8 "Proposition 4.8. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")

###### Proposition [4.8](#S4.Thmtheorem8 "Proposition 4.8. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").

In a $`\delta`$-CSP game $`G`$ the following hold

1.  1.
    Any CCE of $`G`$ is a $`2\delta`$-CCE of any
    $`\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$.
2.  2.
    The marginalized strategy profile of any CCE of $`G`$ is a
    $`2n\delta`$-Nash equilibrium of any
    $`\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$.
3.  3.
    The marginalized strategy profile of any CCE is a
    $`2(n+1)\delta`$-Nash equilibrium of $`G`$

###### Proof.

First we prove claim 1. Let $`\check{u}_{i}`$ denote the utility
function of $`i`$ in $`\check{G}`$. Note that
$`\forall\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$ we have
$`|\check{u}_{i}(\rho)-u_{i}(\rho)|\leq\delta\ \forall i\in N`$. Let
$`\mu`$ be any CCE of $`G`$. The definition of CCE states

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})-u_{i}(\rho)\right]\leq 0\quad\forall i\in N,\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}.`$ |  |

It is sufficient to consider only player $`i`$. We can preserve the
inequality by substituting
$`\check{u}_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})-\delta`$ in place of
$`u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})`$ and
$`\check{u}_{i}(\rho)+\delta`$ in place of $`u_{i}(\rho)`$. This gives
us

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[\check{u}_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})-\delta-(\check{u}_{i}(\rho)+\delta)\right]\leq 0\quad\forall\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\implies`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[\check{u}_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\rho_{-i})-\check{u}_{i}(\rho)\right]\leq 2\delta\quad\forall\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}.`$ |  |

Thus claim 1 is shown. Claim 2 is an immediate corollary of claim 1 and
Proposition [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 4.3. ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
Lastly, we show claim 3. By claim 2, we have the marginalized strategy
of $`\mu`$, $`s^{\mu}`$, is a $`2n\delta`$-Nash equilibrium of
$`\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$. That is for any $`i\in N`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s_{-i}^{\mu})-\check{u}_{i}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{-i}^{\mu})\leq 2n\delta\quad\forall\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}.`$ |  |

However, since $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP, we may substitute
$`u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})-\delta`$ in place of
$`\check{u}_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s^{\mu}_{-i})`$ and
$`u_{i}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{-i}^{\mu})+\delta`$ in place of
$`\check{u}_{i}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{-i}^{\mu})`$ as preserve the inequality.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left(u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s_{-i}^{\mu})-\delta\right)-\left(u_{i}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{-i}^{\mu})+\delta)\right)\leq 2n\delta\quad\forall\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}.`$ |  |

Rearranging, this gives us

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s_{-i}^{\mu})-u_{i}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{-i}^{\mu})\leq 2n\delta+2\delta=2(n+1)\delta\quad\forall\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}.`$ |  |

∎

### C.4 Proof of Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")

###### Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").

If $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP and
$`\exists\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$ that is
$`(2n\delta,\gamma)`$-subgame stable and $`\mu`$ is a CCE of $`G`$, then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textup{Vul}_{i}\left(s^{\mu},S_{-i}\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta\leq(n-1)\gamma+2\delta,`$ |  |

The proof is largely the same as
Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Theorem 4.6. ‣ 4.2 Subgame Stability ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
with added approximation since $`G`$ is no longer CSP.

###### Proof.

Let $`\check{G}`$ be a polymatrix game that is
$`(2n\delta,\gamma)`$-subgame stable such that
$`\check{G}\in\text{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$. Let $`\check{u}_{i}`$ denote the
utility function of $`i`$ in $`\check{G}`$. By
Proposition [4.8](#S4.Thmtheorem8 "Proposition 4.8. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
$`\mu`$ is a $`2n\delta`$-Nash equilibrium of $`\check{G}`$. Then,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textup{Vul}_{i}\left(s^{\mu},S_{-i}\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq u_{i}(s^{\mu})-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}}u_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{-i}^{\prime})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu})-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}}\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{-i}^{\prime})+2\delta,`$ |  |

since $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP. Then expanding $`\check{u}_{i}`$ across
$`i`$’s subgames we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}}\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j})+2\delta`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\min_{s_{j}^{\prime}\in S_{j}}\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j}^{\prime})+2\delta.`$ |  |

Where, as in
Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Theorem 4.6. ‣ 4.2 Subgame Stability ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
the last line uses the fact that $`\check{G}`$ is polymatrix, $`G_{ij}`$
is constant-sum and $`-i`$ minimize $`i^{\prime}s`$ utility and can do
so by without coordinating. Continuing, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\min_{s_{j}^{\prime}\in S_{j}}\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j}^{\prime})+2\delta`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\left(\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i}^{\mu},s_{j}^{\mu})-\min_{s_{j}^{\prime}\in S_{j}}\check{u}_{i}(s^{\mu}_{i},s_{j}^{\prime})\right)+2\delta`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\gamma+2\delta`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq(n-1)\gamma+2\delta.`$ |  |

Where by $`(2n\delta,\gamma)`$-subgame stability of each $`G_{ij}`$,
$`(s^{\mu}_{i},s^{\mu}_{i})`$ is a $`\gamma`$-Nash of $`G_{ij}`$. By
Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3. ‣ C.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix C Omitted Proofs ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
$`s^{\mu}_{i}`$ can lose at most $`\gamma`$ to a worst case opponent
$`s_{j}^{\prime}`$ in each subgame, since $`\check{G}_{ij}`$ is
two-player constant-sum. ∎

### C.5 Proof of Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")

###### Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").

If $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP in the neighborhood of
$`S^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})`$ and
$`\exists\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G,S^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N}))`$
that is $`\gamma`$-subgame stable in the the neighborhood of
$`S(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$, then for any $`s\in S(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Vul}_{i}\left(s,S_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})\right)\leq|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta\leq(n-1)\gamma+2\delta.`$ |  |

###### Proof.

The proof is very similar to
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
Writing the definition of vulnerability we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Vul}_{i}\left(s,S(\mathcal{A})\right)\doteq u_{i}(s)-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})}u_{i}(s,s_{-i}^{\prime}),`$ |  | (6) |

since $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP in the neighborhood of
$`S^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})`$. Swapping out the utility of $`u_{i}`$
for $`\check{u}`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\eqref{eq: 3.13}\leq\check{u}_{i}(s)-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})}\check{u}_{i}(s_{i},s_{-i}^{\prime})+2\delta`$ |  |

Since $`\check{G}`$ is a polymatrix game,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{i}(s)-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})}\check{u}_{i}(s_{i},s_{-i}^{\prime})+2\delta`$ |  | (7) |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i},s_{j})-\min_{s_{-i}^{\prime}\in S_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})}\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i},s_{j})+2\delta`$ |  | (8) |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i},s_{j})-\min_{s_{j}^{\prime}\in S_{j}(\mathcal{A}_{j})}\check{u}_{ij}(s_{i},s_{j}^{\prime})\right)+2\delta.`$ |  | (9) |

Where, as in
Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Theorem 4.6. ‣ 4.2 Subgame Stability ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
and
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
the last line uses the fact that $`\check{G}`$ is polymatrix, $`G_{ij}`$
is constant-sum and $`-i`$ minimize $`i^{\prime}s`$ utility and can do
so by without coordinating.

Since $`\check{G}`$ is $`\gamma`$-subgame stable in the neighborhood of
$`S(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$ and $`s\in S(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$, then means
$`(s_{i},s_{j})`$ is a $`\gamma`$-Nash for each subgame
$`\check{G}_{ij}`$, so has bounded vulnerability within that subgame.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\eqref{eq: 3.16}\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\gamma\right)+2\delta`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle(n-1)\gamma+2\delta`$ |  |

∎

## Appendix D Normal-Form Algorithms

### D.1 Computing Subgame Stability

Let $`\underline{\hbox{$\gamma$}}`$ be the minimum $`\gamma`$ such that
a CSP game $`G`$ is $`(0,\gamma)`$-subgame stable. How do we compute
$`\underline{\hbox{$\gamma$}}`$? Does it involve computing all
equilibria of $`G`$ and checking their subgame stability? The answer is
no, it can be done in polynomial time in the number of pure strategies.
We next provide an algorithm for computing
$`\underline{\hbox{$\gamma$}}`$. The algorithm involves solving a linear
program for each edge in the graph and each pure strategy of those
players. This linear program takes a pure strategy
$`\rho_{i}^{\prime}`$, and finds a Nash equilibrium of $`G`$ that
maximizes $`i`$’s incentive to deviate to $`\rho_{i}^{\prime}`$ when
*only* considering their utility in $`G_{ij}`$; call this quantity
$`\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}`$. If there are no such Nash
equilibria the solver returns “infeasible”. If the solver does not
return “infeasible”, we update
$`\underline{\hbox{$\gamma$}}=\max_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\max_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}}\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}`$.

 Input: $`G=(N,E,\mathrm{P},u)`$, a polymatrix game

 $`\gamma\leftarrow-\infty`$

 for $`(i,j)\in E`$ do

  for $`\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}`$ do

   if $`\text{LP1}(i,j,\rho_{i}^{\prime})`$ not infeasible then

    $`\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}\leftarrow\text{LP1}(i,j,\rho_{i}^{\prime})`$

    $`\gamma\leftarrow\max(\gamma,\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}})`$

   end if

  end for

  for $`\rho_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{j}`$ do

   if $`\text{LP1}(j,i,\rho_{j}^{\prime})`$ not infeasible then

    $`\gamma_{ji}^{\rho_{j}^{\prime}}\leftarrow\text{LP1}(j,i,\rho_{j}^{\prime})`$

    $`\gamma\leftarrow\max(\gamma,\gamma_{ji}^{\rho_{j}^{\prime}})`$

   end if

  end for

 end for

 return $`\gamma`$

Algorithm 2 Compute $`\gamma`$

Let $`a_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\mu)`$ be the advantage of deviating to
$`\rho_{i}^{\prime}`$ from a joint distribution over pure strategies:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\mu)\doteq\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\underbrace{u_{ij}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s_{j}^{\mu})}_{(a)}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}u_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})\right]}_{(b)}`$ |  |

Note that $`(a)`$ is a linear function of $`\mu`$, since $`s_{j}^{\mu}`$
is a marginal strategy. $`(b)`$ is also a linear function of $`\mu`$,
and so $`a_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\mu)`$ is a linear function of $`\mu`$.
Likewise, let

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{ij}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\mu)\doteq u_{ij}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},s_{j}^{\mu})-\mathbb{E}_{\rho\sim\mu}\left[u_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})\right].`$ |  |

be the advantage of $`\rho_{i}^{\prime}`$ in the subgame between $`i`$
and $`j`$. $`\text{LP1}(i,j,\rho_{i}^{\prime})`$ is given below. The
decision variables are the weights of $`\mu`$ for each
$`\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$ and $`\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}`$.

#### LP 1

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\max\quad`$ | $`\displaystyle\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}`$ |  |
|  | s.t. | $`\displaystyle a_{i}(\rho_{i},\mu)\leq 0\quad\forall i\in N,\rho_{i}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle a_{ij}(\rho_{i}^{\prime},\mu)\geq\gamma_{ij}^{\rho_{i}^{\prime}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{\rho\in\mathrm{P}}\mu(\rho)=1`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mu(\rho)\in[0,1]\quad\forall\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$ |  |

We can get away with computing a CCE rather than targeting Nash
equilibria because the marginals of any CCE are Nash equilibria in CSP
games [Cai et al. (2016)](#bib.bib10).

The whole procedure runs in polynomial time in the size of the game. We
need to solve an LP, which takes polynomial time, at most
$`n^{2}\max_{i\in N}|\mathcal{\mathrm{P}}_{i}|`$ times.

### D.2 Finding Constant-Sum Polymatrix Decomposition

Projecting a game into the space of CSP games with minimum $`\delta`$
can be done with a linear program. Let $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$
be the minimum $`\delta`$ such that $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP. We give a
linear program that finds $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$ and returns a
CSP game $`\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}}(G)`$.
The decision variables are the values of $`\check{u}_{ij}(\rho)`$ for
all $`i\neq j\in N,\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$, $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$
and constants for each subgame $`c_{ij}`$, for all $`i\neq j`$.

#### LP 2

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\min\quad`$ | $`\displaystyle\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$ |  |
|  | s.t. | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(\rho)-\sum_{j\in-i}\check{u}_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})\leq\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}\quad\forall i\in N,\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(\rho)-\sum_{j\in-i}\check{u}_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})\geq-\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}\quad\forall i\in N,\rho\in\mathrm{P}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})+\check{u}_{ji}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})=c_{ij}\quad\forall i\neq j\in N,(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})\in\mathrm{P}_{ij},`$ |  |

## Appendix E Extensive-Form Games

Section [4](#S4 "4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
developed notions of approximately CSP and subgame stable in the context
of normal-form games. Here, we apply these concepts to extensive-form
games. While any extensive-form game has an equivalent induced
normal-form game, analysing properties of an EFG through its induced
normal is intractable for moderately-sized EFGs, since the size the
normal-form representation is exponentially larger.

After background on extensive-form games, we introduce a novel
“extensive-form version” of normal-form polymatrix games, which we call
*poly-EFGs*. The major benefit of poly-EFGs over normal-form polymatrix
games is their efficiently: poly-EFGs are exponentially more compact
than an equivalent normal-form polymatrix game. The results of this
section extend the theory of
Sections [4](#S4 "4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
and
[5](#S5 "5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
using this more efficient representation. We also give a
proof-of-concept showing that poly-EFGs can be used to efficiently
decompose extensive-form games by giving an algorithm for decomposing a
perfect information EFG into a poly-EFG.

### E.1 Background on Extensive-Form Games

We use the imperfect information extensive-form game (EFG) as a model
for sequential multi-agent strategic situations. An imperfect
information extensive-form game is a 10-tuple
$`(N,\mathcal{A},H,Z,A,P,u,\mathcal{I},c,\pi_{c})`$ where $`N`$ is a set
of players; $`\mathcal{A}`$ is a set of actions; $`H`$ is a set of
sequences of actions, called *histories*; $`Z\subseteq H`$ is a set of
terminal histories; $`A:H\to\mathcal{A}`$ is a function that maps a
history to available actions; $`P:H\to N`$ is the player function, which
assigns a player to choose an action at each non-terminal history; u =
$`\{u_{i}\}_{i\in N}`$ is a set of utility functions where
$`u_{i}:Z\to\mathbb{R}`$ is the utility function for player $`i`$;
$`\mathcal{I}=\{\mathcal{I}_{i}\}_{i\in N}`$ where $`\mathcal{I}_{i}`$
is a partition of the set $`\{h\in H:P(h)=i\}`$ such that if
$`h,h^{\prime}\in I\in\mathcal{I}_{i}`$ then $`A(h)=A(h^{\prime})`$. We
call an element $`I\in\mathcal{I}_{i}`$ an information set. The chance
player $`c`$ has a function $`\pi_{c}(a,h)\ \forall h:P(h)=c`$ which
returns the probability of random nature events $`a\in\mathcal{A}`$. Let
$`N_{c}=N\cup\{c\}`$ be the set of players including chance.

For some history $`h`$, the $`j`$th action in $`h`$ is written
$`h_{j}`$. A sub-history of $`h`$ from the $`j`$th to $`k`$th actions is
denoted $`h_{j:k}`$ and we use $`h_{:k}`$ as a short-hand for
$`h_{0:k}`$. If a history $`h^{\prime}`$ is a prefix of history $`h`$,
we write $`h^{\prime}\sqsubseteq h`$ and if $`h^{\prime}`$ is a proper
prefix of $`h`$, we write $`h^{\prime}\sqsubset h`$.

A *pure strategy* in an EFG is a deterministic choice of actions for the
player at every decision point. We use
$`\rho_{i}:\mathcal{I}_{i}\to\mathcal{A}`$ to denote a pure strategy of
player $`i`$, and the set of all pure strategies as $`\mathrm{P}_{i}`$.
Likewise, $`s_{i}\in\Delta(\mathrm{P}_{i})=S_{i}`$ is a *mixed
strategy*, where $`\Delta(X)`$ denotes the set of probability
distributions over a domain $`X`$.

There are an exponential number of pure strategies in the number of
information sets. A *behavior strategy* is a compact representation of
the behavior of an agent that assigns a probability distribution over
actions to each information set. We use
$`\pi_{i}\in\Pi_{i}=(\Delta(A(I)))_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}`$ to denote a
behavior strategy of player $`i`$ and $`\pi_{i}(a,I)`$ as the
probability of playing action $`a`$ at $`I`$. Let $`I(h)`$ be the unique
information set such that $`h\in I`$. We overload
$`\pi_{i}(a,h)=\pi_{i}(a,I(h))`$. We use $`\rho\in\mathrm{P},s\in S`$
and $`\pi\in\Pi`$ to denote pure, mixed and behavior strategy profiles,
respectively. Note that $`\mathrm{P}`$ is a subset of both $`\Pi`$ and
$`S`$.

Given a behavior strategy profile, let

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{i}(h_{1},h_{2},\pi_{i})`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq\prod_{h_{1}\sqsubseteq ha\sqsubseteq h_{2},P(ha)=i}\pi_{i}(a,h)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle p(h_{1},h_{2},\pi)`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq\prod_{i\in N_{c}}p_{i}(h_{1},h_{2},\pi_{i})`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{-i}(h_{1},h_{2},\pi_{-i})`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq\prod_{j\in N_{c}\setminus\{i\}}p_{j}(h_{1},h_{2},\pi_{j})`$ |  |

be the probability of transitioning from history $`h_{1}`$ to $`h_{2}`$
according to $`\pi_{i}`$, $`\pi`$ and $`\pi_{-i}`$, respectively. Let
$`p_{i}(z,\pi_{i}),p_{-i}(z,\pi_{i})`$ and $`p(z,\pi_{i})`$ be
short-hands for
$`p_{i}(\varnothing,z,\pi_{i}),p_{-i}(\varnothing,z,\pi_{-i})`$ and
$`p(\varnothing,z,\pi)`$, respectively, where $`\varnothing`$ is the
empty history.

We define the utility of a behavior strategy as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(\pi)\doteq\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\left[u_{i}(z)\right]=\sum_{z\in Z}p(z,\pi)u_{i}(z)=\sum_{z\in Z}\left(\prod_{i\in N_{c}}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})\right)u_{i}(z).`$ |  |

*Perfect recall* is a common assumption made on the structure of
information sets in EFGs that prevents players from forgetting
information they once possessed. Formally, for any $`h\in I`$ let
$`X_{i}(h)`$ denote the set of $`(I,a)`$ s.t. $`I\in\mathcal{I}_{i}`$
and $`\exists h^{\prime}\in I`$ and $`h^{\prime}a\sqsubseteq h`$. Let
$`X_{-i}(h)`$ be defined analogously for $`-i`$ and $`X(h)`$ for all
players.

###### Definition E.1 (Perfect recall).

If
$`\forall I\in\mathcal{I}_{i},\forall h,h^{\prime}\in I,X_{i}(h)=X_{i}(h^{\prime})`$
then $`i`$ has perfect recall. If all players possess perfect recall in
some EFG $`G`$, we call $`G`$ a game of perfect recall.

In games of perfect recall, the set of behavior strategies and mixed
strategies are equivalent: any behavior strategy can be converted into a
mixed strategy which is outcome equivalent over the set of terminal
histories (i.e. has the same distribution over $`Z`$) and vice-versa.

###### Theorem E.2 ([Kuhn (1953)](#bib.bib26)).

In games of perfect recall, any behavior strategy $`\pi_{i}`$ has an
equivalent mixed strategy $`s_{i}`$ (and vice versa), such that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{i}\sim s_{i}}\left[p_{i}(z,\rho_{i})\right].`$ |  |

Theorem [E.2](#A5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem E.2 ( ( ) ). ‣ E.1 Background on Extensive-Form Games ‣ Appendix E Extensive-Form Games ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
establishes a connection between equilibria in behavior and mixed
strategies: a Nash equilibrium behavior strategy profile implies the
equivalent mixed strategy profile is also a Nash equilibrium in mixed
strategies and vice-versa.

We may also reduce any extensive-form game into an equivalent
normal-form game.

###### Definition E.3 (Induced normal-form).

The *induced normal-form* of an extensive-form game $`G`$ (with utility
functions $`u_{i}`$) is a normal-form game
$`G^{\prime}=(N,\mathrm{P},u^{\prime})`$ such that
$`u_{i}^{\prime}(\rho)=u_{i}(\rho)`$

The induced normal-form of an EFG has players making all decisions
up-front. It is not always practical to construct an induced
normal-form, but the concept is useful for proving things about EFGs.

### E.2 Poly-EFGs

What is the appropriate extension of polymatrix games to EFGs? Given
some $`n`$-player EFG $`G`$, what should the subgame between $`i`$ and
$`j`$ be in the graph? Unlike in normal form games, players act
sequentially, and $`i`$ and $`j`$ may either observe actions or have
their utility impacted by other players. There is additional structure
present in EFGs beyond the players’ pure strategies.

The approach we take is to have an EFG for each pair of players $`i`$
and $`j`$. For simplicity, we assume that each subgame
$`G_{ij}^{\prime}`$ shares the same structure as some $`n`$-player game
$`G`$, but information sets where $`P(I)\notin\{i,j\}`$ now belong to
the chance player $`c`$.

###### Definition E.4 (Subgame).

Let $`G=(N,\mathcal{A},H,Z,A,P,u,\mathcal{I},c,\pi_{c})`$ be some EFG.
We define a *subgame*
$`G_{ij}^{\prime}=(\{i,j\},\mathcal{A},H,Z,A,P^{\prime},(u_{ij}^{\prime},u_{ji}^{\prime}),\mathcal{I},c,\pi_{c}^{\prime})`$
as a structurally identical game to $`G`$ between $`i`$ and $`j`$ with
player function $`P^{\prime}`$ and utility functions
$`(u_{ij}^{\prime},u_{ji}^{\prime})`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P^{\prime}(h)\doteq\begin{cases}P(h)\quad&\text{if}\ P(h)\in\{i,j\}\\
c\quad&\text{o.w.}\end{cases}`$ |  |

and let $`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$ be the strategy of the chance player in
$`G^{\prime}_{ij}`$. We put no restrictions on $`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$.

Note that $`u^{\prime}_{ij},u^{\prime}_{ji}`$ are not necessarily
defined in the above definition. They may take any values. We merely
want the subgame $`G_{ij}^{\prime}`$ to share the structure of $`G`$. In
$`G_{ij}^{\prime}`$, $`i`$ and $`j`$’s utility only depends on their
strategies $`\pi_{i},\pi_{j}`$ and chance’s actions
$`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u^{\prime}_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq\mathbb{E}_{z\sim(\pi_{i},\pi_{j},\pi_{j})}\left[u^{\prime}_{ij}(z)\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})u_{ij}^{\prime}(z).`$ |  |

What should $`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$ be defined as? This turns out to not
matter very much. Given any subgame $`G_{ij}^{\prime}`$ with chance
strategy $`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$ and utility functions
$`u_{ij}^{\prime},u_{ji}^{\prime}`$, for any $`G_{ij}^{\prime\prime}`$
with chance strategy $`\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime}`$, we can find
$`u_{ij}^{\prime\prime},u_{ji}^{\prime\prime}`$ so that the utility of
players between the two games will always be equal for any strategy
profile $`(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$.

###### Definition E.5.

We say $`\pi_{c}`$ is *fully mixed* if
$`\pi_{c}^{\prime}(a,h)>0\ \forall h\in\{h\in H\mid P(h)=c\},a\in A(h)`$

###### Proposition E.6.

Let $`G`$ be an EFG and $`G_{ij}^{\prime}`$ a subgame between $`i`$ and
$`j`$ with utility functions $`u^{\prime}_{ij},u^{\prime}_{ji}`$ and
fully mixed chance strategy $`\pi_{c}^{\prime}`$. Given
$`G_{ij}^{\prime\prime}`$, a subgame between $`i`$ and $`j`$ with fully
mixed chance strategy $`\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime}`$, we may find
$`u^{\prime\prime}_{ij},u^{\prime\prime}_{ji}`$ such that
$`\forall\pi_{i},\pi_{j}`$ we have
$`u_{ij}^{\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})=u_{ij}^{\prime\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$
and
$`u_{ji}^{\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})=u_{ji}^{\prime\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$.

###### Proof.

Note that
$`p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime}),p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime})\neq 0`$.
Then $`\forall z\in Z`$, define
$`u_{ij}^{\prime\prime}(z)=\frac{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})}{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime})}u_{ij}^{\prime}(z)`$
and
$`u_{ji}^{\prime\prime}(z)=\frac{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})}{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime})}u_{ji}^{\prime}(z)`$.
Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{ij}^{\prime\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi^{\prime\prime}_{c})u_{ij}^{\prime\prime}(z)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi^{\prime\prime}_{c})\frac{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})}{p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime\prime})}u_{ij}^{\prime}(z)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})u_{ij}^{\prime}(z)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=u_{ij}^{\prime}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j}).`$ |  |

∎

For the remainder of this work, when defining a subgame between $`i`$
and $`j`$ given an EFG $`G`$, we define the subgame chance player’s
strategy to be equal to $`\pi_{c}`$ in $`G`$ at information sets $`I`$
where $`P(I)=c`$ in $`G`$ and uniform randomly otherwise.

Having defined subgames, we may now define our representation of
extensive-form polymatrix games.

###### Definition E.7 (Poly-EFG).

A poly-EFG $`(N,E,\mathcal{G})`$ is defined by a graph with nodes $`N`$,
one for each player, a set of edges $`E`$ and a set of games
$`\mathcal{G}=\{G_{ij}\mid\forall(i,j)\in E\}`$ where
$`G_{ij}\in\mathcal{G}`$ is a two player EFG between $`i`$ and $`j`$ and
all $`G_{ij}\in\mathcal{G}`$ are a subgame between $`i`$ and $`j`$ and
all subgames are defined with respect to some EFG $`G`$.

Let $`G_{ij}\in\mathcal{G}`$ denote the subgame between $`i`$ and $`j`$.
We use subscript $`ij`$ (e.g. $`Z_{ij}`$) to refer to parts of
$`G_{ij}`$.

Since each subgame of the poly-EFG is the subgame of the same $`G`$, the
space of pure, mixed and behavior strategies is the same for each
subgame for any player. A player chooses a strategy (whether pure, mixed
or behavior) and plays this strategy in each subgame. A player’s global
utility is the sum of their utility in each of their subgames. We have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(\pi)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}u_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j}),`$ |  |

where $`E_{i}\subseteq E`$ is the set of edges connected to $`i`$ in the
graph and $`u_{ij}`$ is the utility function of $`i`$ in subgame
$`G_{ij}`$.

### E.3 Constant-Sum and Subgame Stable Poly-EFGs

Here, we give definitions of constant-sum and subgame stability for
poly-EFGs. These definitions are largely identical to their normal-form
counterparts, we merely provide them here for completeness.

Poly-EFGs are constant-sum if, for each subgame, the utilities at the
terminals add up to a constant.

###### Definition E.8 (Constant-sum).

We say a poly-EFG $`G`$ is constant-sum if
$`\forall G_{ij}\in\mathcal{G},z\in Z_{ij}`$,
$`u_{ij}(z)+u_{ji}(z)=c_{ij}`$ where $`Z_{ij}`$ is the set of terminal
histories of $`\forall G_{ij}`$ and $`c_{ij}`$ is a constant.

We may also define approximate poly-EFGs in the same way as in
normal-form games.

###### Definition E.9 ($`\delta`$-constant sum poly-EFG).

An EFG $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-constant sum poly-EFG ($`\delta`$-CSP) if
there exists a constant-sum poly-EFG $`\check{G}`$ with global utility
function $`\check{u}`$ such that $`\forall i\in N,\pi\in\Pi`$,
$`|u_{i}(\pi)-\check{u}_{i}(\pi)|\leq\delta`$. We denote the set of such
CSP games as $`\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$.

Finally, we define subgame stability for poly-EFGs. Our definitions are
near-identical from the normal-form definitions.

###### Definition E.10 (Subgame stable profile).

Let $`G`$ be a poly-EFG. We say a strategy profile $`\pi`$ is
$`\gamma`$-subgame stable if $`\forall(i,j)\in E`$, we have
$`(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ is a $`\gamma`$-Nash of $`G_{ij}`$.

###### Definition E.11 (Subgame stable game).

Let $`G`$ be a poly-EFG. We say $`G`$ is $`(\epsilon,\gamma)`$-subgame
stable if for *any* $`\epsilon`$-Nash equilibrium $`\pi`$ of $`G`$,
$`\pi`$ is $`\gamma`$-subgame stable.

### E.4 Theoretical Results For Poly-EFGs

Our theoretical results from
Sections [4](#S4 "4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
and
[5](#S5 "5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
continue to hold in poly-EFGs. The idea is to use the induced
normal-form of a poly-EFG. We assume perfect recall.

First, we will characterize what self-play will produce in EFGs. These
are called *marginal behavior strategies*.

###### Definition E.12 (Marginal behavior strategy).

Given some mediated equilibrium $`(\mu,(\Phi_{i})_{i=1}^{N})`$, let
$`\pi_{i}^{\mu}`$ be the *marginal behavior strategy* for $`i`$ where
$`\pi_{i}^{\mu}(a,I)`$ is defined arbitrarily if
$`\sum_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}(I)}s_{i}^{\mu}(\rho_{i}^{\prime})=0`$
and otherwise

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi_{i}^{\mu}(a,I)\doteq\frac{\sum_{\rho_{i}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}(a,I)}s_{i}^{\mu}(\rho_{i})}{\sum_{\rho_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{P}_{i}(I)}s_{i}^{\mu}(\rho_{i}^{\prime})}\quad\forall I\in\mathcal{I}_{i},a\in A(I),`$ |  |

where
$`s_{i}^{\mu}(\rho_{i})\doteq\sum_{\rho_{-i}\in\mathrm{P}_{-i}}\mu(\rho_{i},\rho_{-i})`$.

###### Definition E.13 (Marginal behavior strategy profile).

Given some mediated equilibrium $`(\mu,(\Phi_{i})_{i=1}^{N})`$, let
$`\pi^{\mu}`$ be a *marginal behavior strategy profile*, where
$`\pi_{i}^{\mu}`$ is a marginal behavior strategy $`\forall i\in N`$.

###### Definition E.14 (Induced normal-form polymatrix game).

Given a poly-EFG $`G=(N,E,\mathcal{G})`$, the *induced normal-form
polymatrix game* is a polymatrix game
$`G^{\prime}=(N,E,\mathrm{P},u^{\prime})`$ such that $`\mathrm{P}_{i}`$
is equal to $`i`$’s set of pure strategies in each $`G_{ij}`$ and
$`u_{ij}^{\prime}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})=u_{ij}(\rho_{i},\rho_{j})=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\rho_{i})p_{j}(z,\rho_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi_{c}^{\prime})u_{ij}(z)`$
where $`u_{ij}`$ is the utility function of $`i`$ in $`G_{ij}`$.

In games of perfect recall, every behavior strategy $`\pi_{i}`$ has an
equivalent mixed strategy $`s_{i}^{\pi_{i}}`$ (by Kuhn’s Theorem), which
means for any perfect recall EFG $`G`$, we can use the poly-EFG
representation instead of turning $`G`$ into a normal-form game then
using a normal-form polymatrix game to get the same vulnerability bounds
on $`G`$. Given $`\pi`$, let $`s^{\pi}`$ be a profile of equivalent
mixed strategies.

From Kuhn’s Theorem and an assumption that each $`G_{ij}\in\mathcal{G}`$
has perfect recall, we derive two immediate corollaries.

###### Corollary E.15.

If $`\pi`$ is $`\gamma`$ subgame stable for a poly-EFG $`\check{G}`$
where each subgame has perfect recall , then $`s^{\pi}`$ is $`\gamma`$
subgame stable in the induced normal-form polymatrix game of
$`\check{G}`$.

###### Corollary E.16.

For EFG of perfect recall $`G`$, if $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP-EFG then the
induced normal form of $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP.

An extension of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
holds for poly-EFGs. Let $`\Pi^{\mu}`$ be the set of marginal behavior
strategy profiles for any CCE of $`G`$ and $`\Pi^{\mu}_{i}`$ be the set
of marginal behavior strategies for $`i`$.

###### Proposition E.17.

If an EFG $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP and
$`\exists\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G)`$ that is
$`(2n\delta,\gamma)`$-subgame stable and $`\mu`$ is a CCE ⁵⁵ 5 Note that
“CCE” refers to a *normal-form* CCE (NFCCE) in the language of [Farina
et al. (2020)](#bib.bib17). of $`G`$, then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textup{Vul}_{i}\left(\pi^{\mu},\Pi_{-i}\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta\leq(n-1)\gamma+2\delta,`$ |  |

###### Proof.

Transform $`\check{G}`$ into its induced normal-form polymatrix game
$`\check{G}^{\prime}`$. By
Corollaries [E.15](#A5.Thmtheorem15 "Corollary E.15. ‣ E.4 Theoretical Results For Poly-EFGs ‣ Appendix E Extensive-Form Games ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
and
[E.16](#A5.Thmtheorem16 "Corollary E.16. ‣ E.4 Theoretical Results For Poly-EFGs ‣ Appendix E Extensive-Form Games ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
the induced normal form of $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP and
$`(2n\delta,\gamma)`$-subgame stable. By perfect recall, we can convert
$`\pi^{\mu}`$ to an equivalent mixed strategy profile $`s^{\mu}`$ and do
likewise with any $`\pi_{-i}\in\Pi_{-i}`$. Then apply
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9. ‣ 4.3 Approximate Constant-Sum Polymatrix Games ‣ 4 Guarantees via Polymatrix Decomposability ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
using $`s^{\mu}`$, $`S_{-i}`$ and the induced normal-form polymatrix
game of $`\check{G}`$ to bound vulnerability on $`G`$’s induced normal
form, and hence $`G`$. ∎

### E.5 Vulnerability Against Self-Taught Agents in EFGs

Next we show an analogue of
Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
for extensive-form games. In
Section [5](#S5 "5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
we defined $`S(\mathcal{A})`$ as the set of marginal strategy profiles
for a no-regret learning algorithm $`\mathcal{A}`$. Many algorithms for
EFGs will compute behavior strategies, so we use
$`\Pi(\mathcal{A})\doteq\{\pi^{\mu}\mid\ (\mu,(\Phi_{i})_{i\in N})\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A})\}`$
as the set of marginal behavior strategy profiles of
$`\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A})`$ (recall that $`\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A})`$
is the set of mediated equilibria reachable by learning algorithm
$`\mathcal{A}`$. Then let
$`\Pi_{i}(\mathcal{A})\doteq\{\pi_{i}\mid\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal{A})\}`$ be
the set of $`i`$’s marginal strategies from $`\Pi(\mathcal{A})`$. For
example, if $`\mathcal{A}`$ is CFR, $`\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A})`$ is the
set of observably sequentially rational CFCCE [Morrill et al.
(2021b)](#bib.bib34) and $`\Pi(\mathcal{A})`$ is the set of behavior
strategy profiles computable by CFR. Next, suppose each player $`i`$
learns with their own self-play algorithm $`\mathcal{A}_{i}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{A}_{N}\doteq(\mathcal{A}_{1},...\mathcal{A}_{n})`$ be the
profile of learning algorithms;
$`\Pi^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})\doteq\bigtimes_{i\in N}\Pi_{i}(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$
be the set of all possible match-ups between strategies learned in
self-play by those learning algorithms and
$`\Pi^{\times}_{-i}(\mathcal{A}_{N})\doteq\bigtimes_{j\in-i}\Pi_{j}(\mathcal{A}_{j})`$
be the profiles of $`-i`$ amongst these match-ups.

###### Definition E.18.

We say a game $`G`$ is *$`\delta`$-CSP in the neighborhood of
$`\Pi^{\prime}\subseteq\Pi`$* if there exists a constant sum poly-EFG
$`\check{G}`$ such that $`\forall\pi\in\Pi^{\prime}`$ we have
$`\left|u_{i}(\pi)-\check{u}_{i}(\pi)\right|\leq\delta`$. We denote the
set of such CSP games as $`\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G,\Pi^{\prime})`$.

###### Definition E.19.

We say a poly-EFG game $`G`$ is *$`\gamma`$-subgame stable in the
neighborhood of $`\Pi^{\prime}`$* if
$`\forall\pi\in\Pi^{\prime},\forall(i,j)\in E`$ we have that
$`(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ is a $`\gamma`$-Nash of $`G_{ij}`$.

###### Proposition E.20.

If $`G`$ is $`\delta`$-CSP in the neighborhood of
$`\Pi^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})`$ and
$`\exists\check{G}\in\mathrm{CSP}_{\delta}(G,\Pi^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N}))`$
that is $`\gamma`$-subgame stable in the the neighborhood of
$`\Pi(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$ , then for any $`\Pi\in\Pi(\mathcal{A}_{i})`$

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Vul}_{i}\left(\pi,\Pi_{-i}^{\times}(\mathcal{A}_{N})\right)\leq|E_{i}|\gamma+2\delta\leq(n-1)\gamma+2\delta.`$ |  |

The proof goes the same way as in
Corollary [E.17](#A5.Thmtheorem17 "Proposition E.17. ‣ E.4 Theoretical Results For Poly-EFGs ‣ Appendix E Extensive-Form Games ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
Use the induced normal-form polymatrix game of $`\check{G}`$ and
Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5 Vulnerability Against Other Self-Taught Agents ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
to derive bounds for the induced normal form of $`G`$, which then apply
to $`G`$.

### E.6 Leveraging the Poly-EFG Representation for Computing CSP Decompositions

The poly-EFG representation gives rise to more efficient algorithms for
computing a poly-EFG decomposition. As a proof of concept, we show that
in perfect information EFGs, we can write a linear program to compute
the optimal polymatrix decomposition for an EFG that is exponentially
smaller than LP 2 from
Section [D.2](#A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "LP 2 ‣ D.2 Finding Constant-Sum Polymatrix Decomposition ‣ Appendix D Normal-Form Algorithms ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
Recall that $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$ is the *minimum* value of
$`\delta`$ such that a game is $`\delta`$-CSP. In an perfect information
EFG, we can compute $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$ with the following
LP. The decision variables are $`\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$, the
values of $`\check{u}_{ij}(z)\ \forall z\in Z,(i,j)\in E`$ and
$`c_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in E`$.

#### LP 3

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\min\quad`$ | $`\displaystyle\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}`$ |  |
|  | s.t. | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(z)-\sum_{j\in-i}\check{u}_{ij}(z)\leq\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}\quad\forall i\in N,z\in Z`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle u_{i}(z)-\sum_{j\in-i}\check{u}_{ij}(z)\geq-\underline{\hbox{$\delta$}}\quad\forall i\in N,z\in Z`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{ij}(z)+\check{u}_{ji}(z)=c_{ij}\quad\forall i\neq j\in N,z\in Z`$ |  |

The trick is that in perfect information EFGs, each pure strategy
profile leads to a single terminal. Hence, rather than having a
constraint for each pure strategy profile, a constraint for each
terminal will suffice. This leads to an exponential reduction in the
number of constraints over LP 2.

## Appendix F Details of SGDecompose

Next, we give the full details of SGDecompose. We give details here
using our poly-EFG representation, since this is the representation we
use in our experiments.

For each subgame $`\check{G}_{ij}`$ we store a single vector
$`\check{u}_{ij}`$ where the entry $`\check{u}_{ij}(z)`$ gives the value
of the utility for corresponding terminal $`z`$. We additionally store a
constant $`\check{c}_{ij}`$ for each subgame. Player $`i`$ will use
$`\check{u}_{ij}`$ when computing $`\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi_{c})\check{u}_{ij}(z).`$ |  |

Whereas we compute $`\check{u}_{ji}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ as follows.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}_{ji}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})=\sum_{z\in Z}p_{i}(z,\pi_{i})p_{j}(z,\pi_{j})p_{c}(z,\pi_{c})\left(\check{c}_{ij}-\check{u}_{ij}(z)\right).`$ |  |

For simplicity, let $`\check{u}`$ denote the stacked vector of all
$`\check{u}_{ij}`$ and $`\check{c}_{ij}`$. We additionally initialize
$`\check{G}`$ as a fully connected graph.

The overall loss function which we minimize has two components: first,
$`\mathcal{L}^{\delta}`$ is the error between the utility functions of
$`G`$ and $`\check{G}`$; it is a proxy for $`\delta`$ in $`\delta`$-CSP.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\delta}\left(\pi;\check{u},u\right)`$ | $`\displaystyle\doteq\sum_{i\in N}\left|\check{u}_{i}(\pi)-u_{i}(\pi)\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in N}\left|\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})\right)-u_{i}(\pi)\right|.`$ |  |

The other component of the overall loss function,
$`\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}`$, measures the subgame stability. First, we
define $`\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}_{ij}`$, which only applies to a single
subgame.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}_{ij}(\pi_{ij},\pi_{ij}^{*};\check{u})\doteq`$ | $`\displaystyle\max\left(\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i}^{*},\pi_{j})-\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{ij}),0\right)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle+`$ | $`\displaystyle\max\left(\check{u}_{ji}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j}^{*})-\check{u}_{ji}(\pi_{ij}),0\right).`$ |  |

Where $`\pi_{ij}=(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})`$ is a profile and
$`\pi^{*}_{ij}=(\pi_{i}^{*},\pi_{j}^{*})`$ is a profile of deviations.
Then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}\left(\pi,\pi^{*};\check{u}\right)\doteq\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}_{ij}(\pi_{ij},\pi_{ij}^{*};\check{u}).`$ |  |

Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix F Details of SGDecompose ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows how to compute a subgame stable constant-sum polymatrix
decomposition via SGD. As input, the algorithm receives a game $`G`$, a
finite set of strategy profiles $`\Pi^{\prime}`$, learning rate
$`\eta`$, number of training epochs $`T`$, hyperparameter
$`\lambda\in[0,1]`$ and batch size $`B`$. First, we initialize
$`\Pi^{\times}`$ as the set of all match-ups amongst strategies in
$`\Pi^{\prime}`$.

We then repeat the following steps for each epoch. First, we compute a
best-response (for example, via sequence-form linear programming) to
each strategy $`\pi^{\prime}_{i}`$ in $`\Pi^{\prime}`$ in each subgame;
the full process is shown in
Algorithm [4](#alg4 "Algorithm 4 ‣ Appendix F Details of SGDecompose ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
After computing these best-responses for the current utility function of
$`\check{G}`$, we try to fit $`\check{u}`$ to be nearly CSP in the
neighborhood of $`\Pi^{\times}`$ and subgame stable in the neighborhood
of $`\Pi^{\prime}`$. Since $`\Pi^{\times}`$ is exponentially larger than
$`\Pi^{\prime}`$, we partition it into batches, then use batch gradient
descent. We use the following batch loss function, which computes the
average values of $`\mathcal{L}^{\delta}`$ and $`\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}`$
over the batches, then weights the losses with $`\lambda`$. Let
$`\Pi^{b}`$ denote a batch of strategy profiles from $`\Pi^{\times}`$
with size $`B`$, the overall loss function is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\Pi^{b},\Pi^{\prime},\Pi^{*};\check{u},u)\doteq\frac{\lambda}{B}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi^{b}}\mathcal{L}^{\delta}(\pi;\check{u},u)+\frac{(1-\lambda)}{|\Pi^{\prime}|}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi^{\prime}}\sum_{\pi^{*}\in\Pi^{*}}\mathcal{L}^{\gamma}(\pi,\pi^{*};\check{u}).`$ |  |

We take this loss and find its gradient with respect to $`\check{u}`$,
then update $`\check{u}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}\leftarrow\check{u}-\eta\cdot\nabla_{\check{u}}\mathcal{L}(\Pi^{b},\Pi^{\prime},\Pi^{*};\check{u},u).`$ |  |

We found that in practise the gradient can be quite large relative to
$`\check{u}`$, which has the potential to destabilize optimization. This
is alleviated by normalizing the gradient by its $`l^{2}`$ norm.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle g`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\nabla_{\check{u}}\mathcal{L}(\Pi^{b},\Pi^{\prime},\Pi^{*};\check{u},u)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\check{u}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\check{u}-\eta\cdot\frac{g}{\left\lVert g\right\rVert}_{2}`$ |  |

 Input: $`G`$, $`\Pi^{\prime}`$, $`\eta`$, $`T`$, $`\lambda`$, $`B`$

 Initialize $`\check{u}`$ to all $`0`$

 $`\Pi^{\times}\leftarrow\bigtimes_{i\in N}\hat{\Pi}_{i}`$

 for $`t\in 1...T`$ do

  $`\Pi^{*}\leftarrow`$ getBRs($`\check{G}`$, $`\Pi^{\prime}`$)

  $`\mathcal{B}\leftarrow`$ partition of $`\Pi^{\times}`$ into batches
of size $`B`$

  for $`\Pi^{b}\in\mathcal{B}`$ do

   $`g\leftarrow\nabla_{\check{u}}\mathcal{L}(\Pi^{b},\Pi^{\prime},\Pi^{*};\check{u},u)`$

   $`\check{u}\leftarrow\check{u}-\eta\cdot\frac{g}{\left\lVert g\right\rVert}_{2}`$

  end for

 end for{Lastly, output $`\delta`$ and $`\gamma`$}

 $`\delta\leftarrow\max_{\pi\in\Pi^{\times}}\left|u_{i}(\pi)-\check{u}_{i}(\pi)\right|`$

 $`\gamma\leftarrow\max_{\pi\in\Pi^{\prime}}\max_{i\neq j\in N\times N}\left(\check{u}_{ij}(BR_{ij}(\pi_{j}),\pi_{j})-\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})\right)`$

 return $`\check{u},\gamma,\delta`$

Algorithm 3 SGDecompose with behavior strategies

 Input: $`\check{G}`$, $`\Pi^{\prime}`$

 $`\Pi_{i}^{*}\leftarrow\varnothing\ \forall i\in N`$

 for $`i\neq j\in N\times N`$ do

  for $`\pi_{j}\in\Pi^{\prime}_{j}`$ do

   compute
$`\pi_{ij}^{*}\in\argmax_{\pi_{i}^{\prime}\in\Pi_{i}}\check{u}_{ij}(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\pi_{j})`$

   $`\Pi_{i}^{*}\leftarrow\Pi_{i}^{*}\cup\{\pi_{ij}^{*}\}`$

  end for

 end for

 return $`\bigtimes_{i\in N}\Pi_{i}^{*}`$

Algorithm 4 getBRs

## Appendix G Experiment Details

The codebase for our experiments is available at
[https://github.com/RevanMacQueen/Self-Play-Polymatrix](https://github.com/RevanMacQueen/Self-Play-Polymatrix).

### G.1 Leduc Poker

We ran SGDecompose 30 times, each time with its own set of 30 strategy
profiles. These 900 strategy profiles are generated with CFR+ in
self-play for 1000 iterations with random initializations. We randomly
initialize CFR+ with regrets between 0 and 0.001 chosen uniformly at
random, which are the default values in OpenSpiel.

Interestingly, we found that CFR+ converges to approximate Nash
equilibria in Leduc poker, with a maximum value of $`\epsilon`$ equal to
$`0.013`$ after 1000 iterations. As we will show in
Appendix [G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 CFR Finds Approximate Nash in Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability"),
CFR also empirically produces approximate Nash equilibria in Leduc
poker.

Let $`\Pi(\mathrm{CFR}+)_{j}`$ denote the set of
$`\mathrm{CFR}+`$-learned strategy profiles for run $`j`$; and
$`\Pi^{\times}(\mathrm{CFR}+)_{j}`$ denote the set of all match-ups
between these 30 strategy profiles.
Figure [5](#A7.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ G.1 Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows diversity of $`\Pi(\mathrm{CFR}+)_{j}`$ for each of the 30 runs.
We measure the diversity of each $`\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}`$ by taking
each pair of strategy profiles
$`\pi,\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}`$ and computing the total
variation between these two probability distributions induced over the
terminal histories of Leduc poker. We denote the maximum total variation
for run $`j`$ as $`TV_{j}`$, where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle TV_{j}\doteq\max_{\pi,\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{z\in Z}|p(z,\pi)-p(z,\pi^{\prime})|.`$ |  |

$`TV_{j}`$ is constrained to be between $`0`$ and $`1`$, where $`0`$
means the two distributions are the same and $`1`$ means they are
maximally different.
Figure [5](#A7.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ G.1 Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows the maximum total variation between any two of the strategy
profiles used in each run.

Figure 5: The maximum total variation for each $`\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}`$
used in different runs of SGDecompose in Leduc Poker. Different runs are
shown on the x-axis, and the corresponding $`TV_{j}`$ for run $`j`$ is
shown with the bars. A value of $`0`$ indicates minimal diversity and
$`1`$ means maximal diversity. The minimum, mean, maximum and standard
error across runs are $`0.21`$, $`0.22`$, $`0.26`$ and $`0.0016`$,
respectively.

We used the same parameters for each run of SGDecompose:
$`\lambda=0.5`$, $`B=30`$, $`T=200`$. We used a learning rate schedule
where the learning rate $`\eta`$ begins at $`2^{-6}`$, then halves every
5 epochs until reaching $`2^{-17}`$ to encourage convergence. Our
results are shown in
Figure [6](#A7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ G.1 Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
We see that across the 30 runs of SGDecompose, Leduc poker is at most
$`0.021`$-CSP in the neighborhood of $`\Pi^{\times}(\mathrm{CFR}+)_{j}`$
and $`0.009`$-subgame stable in the neighborhood of
$`\Pi(\mathrm{CFR}+)_{j}`$.
Figure [7](#A7.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ G.1 Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows the maximum vulnerability with respect to the strategies in each
of the runs compared to the bounds on vulnerability given by
Proposition [E.20](#A5.Thmtheorem20 "Proposition E.20. ‣ E.5 Vulnerability Against Self-Taught Agents in EFGs ‣ Appendix E Extensive-Form Games ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
We compute the maximum vulnerability as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{Vul}_{j}\doteq\max_{i\in N}\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}}\mathrm{Vul}_{i}\left(\pi,\Pi_{-i}^{\times}(\mathrm{CFR})_{j}\right).`$ |  | (10) |

We see that the bounds are between $`1.89`$ and $`3.05`$ times the
actual vulnerability, and are on average $`2.51`$ times larger with a
standard error of $`0.049`$.

(b)

### G.2 CFR Finds Approximate Nash in Leduc Poker

(a)

(b)

Figure 8: CFR empirically computes Nash Equilibria in Leduc Poker. (a)
shows learning curves over iterations for each of the players. We
measure $`\epsilon`$ by finding a best-response with sequence-form
linear programming every 1000 iterations. We show each of the individual
instances of CFR with different random initializations in light-coloured
lines and the average across seeds in bold. (b) shows the distribution
of $`\epsilon`$ at iteration 10,000.

It was previously believed that CFR does not compute an
$`\epsilon`$-Nash equilibrium on 3-player Leduc for any reasonable value
of $`\epsilon`$. Previous work found that CFR computed a $`0.130`$-Nash
equilibrium after $`10^{8}`$ iterations [Abou Risk & Szafron
(2010)](#bib.bib1). We saw in the previous section that
$`\mathrm{CFR}+`$ computes approximate Nash equilibria in Leduc
poker—does this hold for $`\mathrm{CFR}`$ as well?

We ran $`30`$ runs of $`\mathrm{CFR}`$ in self-play for 10,000
iterations and found that *all* of our strategies converged to an
approximate Nash equilibrium with the maximum $`\epsilon=0.017`$ after
only $`10^{4}`$ iterations.
Figure [8(b)](#A7.F8.sf2 "In Figure 8 ‣ G.2 CFR Finds Approximate Nash in Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows the shows the maximum deviation incentive

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\epsilon=\max_{\pi_{i}^{\prime}}u_{i}(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\pi_{-i})-u_{i}(\pi)`$ |  |

for each of the CFR strategies $`\pi`$ computed by CFR in Leduc Poker.
Each column is for one of the players and each point is one of the
random seeds. We see the maximum value of $`\epsilon`$ after 10,000
iterations is $`0.017`$.
Figure [8(a)](#A7.F8.sf1 "In Figure 8 ‣ G.2 CFR Finds Approximate Nash in Leduc Poker ‣ Appendix G Experiment Details ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability")
shows the maximum deviation incentive $`\epsilon`$ over 10,000
iterations. We average learning curves over 30 random seeds.

## Appendix H Toy Hanabi

In games with low values of $`\delta`$ and $`\gamma`$, self-play will
perform well against new opponents; however is the converse also true?
Do games where self-play performs poorly against new opponents have high
values of $`\delta`$ and $`\gamma`$? As mentioned earlier, self-play
struggles to generalize to new agents in some games with specialized
conventions ([Hu et al., 2020](#bib.bib22)). Hanabi is one such game
([Bard et al., 2020](#bib.bib5)). Hanabi is a cooperative game where
players cannot see their own hands, but can see all other players hands;
therefore players must give each other hints on how to act.

We show that a small version of the game of Hanabi is not close to the
space of CSP games and self-play is quite vulnerable. We use Tiny Hanabi
in the Openspiel framework ([Lanctot et al., 2019](#bib.bib28)) with our
own payoffs, shown in
Figure [9](#A8.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix H Toy Hanabi ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
Chance deals one of two hands, $`A`$ or $`B`$ with equal probability.
Only player $`1`$ may observe this hand and must signal to other players
through their actions, $`\sigma_{1}`$ and $`\sigma_{2}`$, which hand
chance has dealt. If both players $`2`$ and $`3`$ then correctly choose
their actions to match chance’s deal ($`(a,a)`$ for $`A`$ or $`(b,b)`$
for $`B`$) then all players get payoff equal to $`1`$, otherwise all
players get $`0`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 9: Tiny Hanabi. We omit payoffs of $`0`$ at terminals.

$`\sigma_{1}`$ and $`\sigma_{2}`$ can come to mean different things,
$`\sigma_{1}`$ could signal to $`2`$ and $`3`$ to play $`a`$, or $`b`$.
Self-play may learn either of these conventions. However, if a player
trained in self-play encounters a set of players trained in an
independent instance of self-play, they may not have compatible
conventions.

This is indeed what happens when we train CFR on Tiny Hanabi in
Figure [9](#A8.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix H Toy Hanabi ‣ Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability").
We trained 30 runs in self-play with different random initializations
for 10,000 iterations. Some of these runs converged to each convention
and when played against each other miscoordinated. We found

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\max_{i\in N}\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathrm{CFR})}\mathrm{Vul}_{i}\left(\pi,\Pi_{-i}^{\times}(\mathrm{CFR})\right)\approx 1,`$ |  |

as expected.

We decomposed Tiny Hanabi and found $`\delta=0.5`$ and
$`\gamma\approx 0`$, meaning the true vulnerability matched what our
bounds predicted since $`(n-1)\gamma+2\delta\approx 1`$. Why is
$`\gamma\approx 0`$? We found that this was because our algorithm was
setting the payoffs to equal to $`0.50`$ for all terminal histories,
which is trivially polymatrix.
````
